summary:
Guam is an unincorporated territory of the United States, and federal law applies there as it does in the states. Local law adds its own non-discrimination protections and its own conditions for changing identity documents.

Private, consensual, non-commercial sexual conduct between adults has been lawful since the Criminal Code was reformed in 1978. The code it replaced, imposed by the Naval Governor in 1933 and modelled on California's, criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus regardless of the sexes of the parties, with sentences of one to ten years. The only reported sodomy prosecution in Guam, in the early 1950s, ended when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had no authority to try the defendant without a jury.

Guam was the first United States territory to recognise marriage between two people of the same sex. In April 2015 Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero sued after being refused a licence; on 5 June 2015 Chief Judge Frances M. Tydingco-Gatewood of the District Court of Guam struck down the prohibition, and the ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression is prohibited locally. In August 2015 the Guam Legislature passed Bill 102-33 unanimously, banning discrimination in private employment on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and separately barring discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Federal hate-crime law has covered offences motivated by gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act, and that coverage reaches Guam.

Changing legal gender is tied to surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a trans person must file a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery with the Office of Vital Statistics, which then amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

A 2018 attempt to remove the surgical requirement failed. In May 2018 Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill permitting legal gender change with judicial permission and a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 so that medical and law-enforcement process issues could be addressed, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by six votes to seven.

Social attitudes are described as permissive. The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people, and homosexuality was taken for granted as part of life rather than treated as taboo. Contemporary accounts describe Guam as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment, though that assessment is general to LGBTQ people rather than specific to transgender residents and visitors.

An LGBTQ social scene has been visible since the 1990s, with a handful of nightclubs and social functions, and an annual pride event has been held since 2017, drawing a few hundred people. Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun marketing itself as a destination for LGBTQ tourists.
tangentialFactors: Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so federal rules governing military service bear directly on a substantial local population. A January 2025 executive order bars transgender troops from serving openly, frames trans identity as radical gender ideology, and directed the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days. The order applies in Guam.
localsOnly:
Residents changing identity documents deal with two separate offices. The Office of Vital Statistics amends a birth certificate on a sworn physician statement confirming sex reassignment surgery; the Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's licence on a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed. Neither route accepts a self-declaration or a non-surgical clinical letter.

Local employment protection covers private-sector workers on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity. The 2018 reform bill would have replaced the surgical test with judicial permission plus a letter from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional; the Legislature postponed the vote on 13 December 2018 over medical and law-enforcement process issues and rejected the bill on 17 December 2018 by six votes to seven.
outOfScopeNotes:
The tolerance finding in the source material is framed as general to LGBTQ people, not specific to transgender people, and no trans-specific discrimination or harassment data for Guam was identified.

No enforcement data was identified for the local employment non-discrimination provisions: complaint volumes, agency practice and outcomes are not sourced.

No local enforcement data was identified for the federal hate-crime coverage of gender identity, and no post-2018 legislative attempt to change the surgical requirement for identity documents appears in the inventory.
